{{Elections in Tennessee}}
The '''2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Tennessee''' will be held on November 8, 2022, to elect the nine [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from the [[U.S. state|state]] of [[Tennessee]], one from each of the state's nine [[Tennessee's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The elections coincide with [[United States House of Representatives elections, 2022|other elections]] to the House of Representatives, [[2022 United States Senate elections|elections]] to the [[United States Senate]] and various [[2022 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2022 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]].

{{see also|Tennessee's 1st congressional district}}
The 1st district is based in northeast Tennessee, encompassing all of [[Carter County, Tennessee|Carter]], [[Cocke County, Tennessee|Cocke]], [[Greene County, Tennessee|Greene]], [[Hamblen County, Tennessee|Hamblen]], [[Hancock County, Tennessee|Hancock]], [[Hawkins County, Tennessee|Hawkins]], [[Johnson County, Tennessee|Johnson]], [[Sullivan County, Tennessee|Sullivan]], [[Unicoi County, Tennessee|Unicoi]], and [[Washington County, Tennessee|Washington]] counties and parts of [[Jefferson County, Tennessee|Jefferson]] and [[Sevier County, Tennessee|Sevier]] counties, and includes the [[Tri-Cities, Tennessee|Tri-Cities]] region. The district was barely impacted by the 2020 redistricting cycle. The incumbent is Republican [[Diana Harshbarger]], who was elected with 74.7% of the vote in 2020.

{{see also|Tennessee's 3rd congressional district}}
The 3rd district encompasses most of the [[Chattanooga metropolitan area|Chattanooga metro]] in east<nowiki/>ern Tennessee, along with several suburban and rural areas near Knoxville and the Tri-Cities. The district was barely impacted by the 2020 redistricting cycle. However, under the new lines, the district no longer touches the border of Tennessee. The incumbent is Republican [[Chuck Fleischmann]], who was re-elected with 67.3% of the vote in 2020.

The 5th district was previously centered on [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] and the immediate surrounding suburbs, but it also contained parts of Cheatham and Dickson county. On January 25, Cooper announced he would withdraw his candidacy for re-election and refund all campaign contributions,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Schelzig|first=Eric|date=January 25, 2022|title=Jim Cooper to retire from Congress after 5th District redistricting|url=https://onthehill.tnjournal.net/jim-cooper-to-retire-from-congress-after-5th-district-redistricting/|archive-date=January 25, 2022|access-date=January 25, 2022|website=The Tennessee Journal}}</ref> citing the state legislature's move to [[gerrymandering|split Davidson County into three congressional districts]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lamb|first=Jason|date=January 24, 2022|title=House Republicans approve congressional redistricting plan|url=https://www.newschannel5.com/news/house-republicans-approve-congressional-redistricting-plan|archive-date=January 24, 2022|access-date=January 25, 2022|website=News Channel 5 Nashville}}</ref> Under the Republican redistricting plan, the new 5th district will shift from D+9 to R+15 and contain only a small Southern part of Nashville, with the 6th and 7th districts absorbing the West and East parts of Davidson county, respectively.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 25, 2022|title=What Redistricting Looks Like In Every State|url=https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/redistricting-2022-maps/tennessee/republican_proposal_2/|archive-date=January 25, 2022|access-date=January 25, 2022|website=FiveThirtyEight}}</ref>

The 9th district is based in [[Memphis, Tennessee|Memphis]]. Redistricting left the 9th district intact, but it moves from having a 53-percentage point Democratic advantage to a 43-point one after taking on some Republican-leaning suburbs. The incumbent is Democrat [[Steve Cohen (politician)|Steve Cohen]], who was re-elected with 77.4% of the vote in 2020.
